entries.title: What does Trump's midterm elections loss mean for strained US-India ties?
entries.summary: Donald Trump's electoral setback might give New Delhi and Washington space to reset relations, but there is no guarantee that the US will actually change its approach to India.
entries.content:
India

What does Trump's midterm loss mean for India-US ties?

November 5, 2026

Donald Trump's electoral setback might give New Delhi and Washington space to reset relations, but there is no guarantee that the US will actually change its approach to India.

With the US Democrats scoring a resounding midterm victory and taking control of both chambers of Congress, the Republican administration led by Donald Trump is set for a new level of scrutiny until the end of Trump's term.

Trump is likely to face pushback on his controversial foreign policy, which saw the US alienate most of its allies and get entangled in yet another unpopular war in the Middle East. At the same time, the Trump administration has also taken a slew of less conspicuous but still highly controversial moves on the global stage, including a series of confrontations with India.

The ties between New Delhi and Washington are still strained by a stalled trade agreement, restrictions on immigration, and disagreement over India buying Russian oil and weapons, despite the US granting an oil ban waiver in March 2026 and Trump waving some of the Russia sanctions in October.

And while the new US Congress can choose to pressure Trump over issues such as tariffs and immigration, the president still wields significant authority on foreign policy.

Congress likely to look into Trump's trade restrictions

The immediate test for Trump's India policy is trade. India and the US have yet to formalize the interim framework discussed by Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi in February, with the two nations still at odds over market access and other trade commitments.

Shanthie Mariet D'Souza, founder of the Mantraya Institute of Strategic Studies, expects the new Congress to apply "increased scrutiny of protectionist measures" pushed by the Trump administration.

The US lawmakers could push for "stronger trade oversight and clearer standards for environmental and labor issues," she told DW.

For India, whose largest export market is the US, this could offer some breathing room.

She also emphasized that "the fundamental pillars of the India-US strategic partnership are expected to remain strong" and "the long-term goal of deepening economic ties is likely to continue."

'The president is not rational'

Immigration presents a different challenge. The administration's tightening of H-1B visa rules, including imposing a $100,000 (€88,761) payment for certain new petitions, has alarmed Indian professionals and tech companies that rely on the visa program to secure jobs in the US.

A Democratic majority could increase scrutiny on that issue as well, but would not automatically reverse measures introduced by Trump's executive action.

"Both parties have bigger issues to grapple with," said Rajkrishna Iyer, a California-licensed immigration lawyer. "For the last 25-plus years, Congress has done nothing for immigration," he added.

Iyer believes that legal immigration itself is not a major priority for voters. Nevertheless, he sees the midterms' result as a message to Trump about his immigration policies.

"A rational president would not spend time imposing further restrictions on legal immigration. But as we know, the president is not rational," Iyer said.

The immigration lawyer believes that new, steep fee for some H-1B applications will be challenged in court.

"Most likely, the new rules will not come into effect. And if they do, federal courts are likely to strike them down because the fees are not reasonable," said Iyer.

While the executive branch of government can raise fees to reflect administrative costs and inflation, Iyer argues that charges of this magnitude could deter people from pursuing legal immigration. "Only Congress can pass such legislation," he said.

US still wants less dependence on Russia

The new balance of power in Washington could also trigger a new geopolitical reshuffle and a change of course on Russia. However, it is unclear if the Democrat-dominated Congress will force any changes in the dispute between New Delhi and Washington over India's purchasing Russian energy. During a congressional vote on Russian sanctions in September, a substantial number of Democrats joined Republican lawmakers to endorse trade restrictions against Moscow.

"Regarding Russian oil, the administration is likely to maintain its preference for reducing dependence on Moscow, but it will approach this issue with diplomatic caution to avoid straining relations with New Delhi," D'Souza says.

India angry over US supplying Pakistan with weapons

The war in Iran adds another dimension. Any new escalation could affect energy exports from the Middle East and make India more vulnerable due to its need for high oil imports.

But Navtej Sarna, a former Indian ambassador to the US and Israel, urges cautions when discussing the future of US policy in the Middle East.

"It may be facile to try and parse these results for their immediate impact on specific areas of foreign policy. Much will depend on how Trump reacts," Sarna told DW.

At the same time, Sarna expects Washington to become "a more contested place," with greater congressional pushback on issues that divide India and the US.

"If that injects some balance and stability and restores institutional linkages it's good for the long-term future of our relationship," he added.

Security cooperation is another stumbling block. New Delhi is still by far the biggest buyer of Russia's arms exports, which irritates Washington. At the same time, India has objected to US supplying weapons to Pakistan, including the $686 million sale of advanced military tech for Pakistan's F-16 jets.

"Washington's military support for Pakistan remains a complex issue. However, ongoing regional adjustments and US concerns about stability in the region will probably prevent any significant policy changes," said D'Souza.

Trump could 'double down' on New Delhi policy

The broader question is whether the election produces a more predictable Washington or a more confrontational Donald Trump.

A weakened president could be more inclined to seek compromises at home. But Trump could also respond to congressional resistance by taking a harder line elsewhere.

"We hope the electoral setback will prompt Trump to undertake a more considered review of his earlier actions," Amitabh Mattoo, dean of the School of International Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University, told DW.

But he also warns that it too early to assess the implications for India-US relations.

"Rather than moderating his approach, the president could double down and adopt an even harder line towards New Delhi if he comes to believe that Indians, particularly sections of the diaspora, played a role, directly or indirectly, in his party's defeat."

Business as usual for US and India?

Harsh Pant of the Observer Research argues that the US president retains considerable leverage over foreign policy despite the Republican setback, and that the India-US partnership has traditionally enjoyed bipartisan support.

"I don't think India will be one of those issues" on which the White House and Congress are likely to clash, Pant told DW.

But the experience of the past two years, he argues, reinforces the need for India to reduce its dependence on any single partner.

"The need for diversification of partnerships, the need to be self-reliant in certain critical sectors, the need to have alternative supply chains — all of those issues remain where they are. The US midterms do not really change the calculus," he says.

entries.title: Pioneering Jewish academy opens in Germany
entries.summary: A Jewish academy has opened its doors in Frankfurt. The Central Council of Jews in Germany, the country’s leading Jewish umbrella group, set up the project to combat hate and promote dialogue and learning nationally.
entries.content:
Germany

Pioneering Jewish academy opens in Germany

November 5, 2026

A Jewish academy has opened its doors in Frankfurt. The Central Council of Jews in Germany, the country’s leading Jewish umbrella group, set up the project to combat hate and promote dialogue and learning nationally.

The western city of Frankfurt was a very conscious choice of location for the new academy, which is the first of its kind in Germany. Frankfurt has traditionally been a hub of Jewish intellectual life — still one of the most important centers of Jewish life in Germany today alongside Berlin, Munich and Düsseldorf.

Less than a 10-minute walk from the city's biggest synagogue, the Jewish Academy is also within sight of the historic festival hall building on Frankfurt Trade Fair grounds where the Nazis herded Jewish men in 1938 and deported them to concentration camps.

It was also here that the Central Council of Jews in Germany was founded in 1950; Berlin serves as its headquarters today. Frankfurt is also home to the Central Welfare Board of Jews in Germany (ZWST) and a Jewish museum that opened in 1988.

Jewish thinkers have played a key role in Frankfurt's intellectual and academic history. The city's Jewish community contributed to the establishment of Goethe University in 1914.

Another important legacy is the Jewish Lehrhaus (house of study). Founded in 1920, it quickly gained prominence and is today associated with the philosopher Franz Rosenzweig (1886–1929). It was closed by the Nazis in 1938. The new academy sees itself in the tradition of Rosenzweig's Lehrhaus.

A place of education and dialogue

Speaking at the opening ceremony on Monday, Josef Schuster, president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, stressed: "We must combat hatred with education, education and more education."

Schuster said the institute was a "milestone” that represented the "Jewish community's determination to call Germany home." At the same time, he emphasized: "Jewish life in Germany is under greater threat than it has been since the crime against humanity that was the Shoah."

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier also underlined the need to reject antisemitism "outright and without reservation." He added that it must also be combated politically.

The federal president said the murder of six million Jews in the Holocaust had also targeted the Jewish world of learning and knowledge. He specifically honored Rosenzweig's legacy: "This place of knowledge and dialogue was a source of hope, something exciting and something new."

A bridge between tradition and modernity, as well as academia and the general public

The Jewish Academy combines traditional features of a 110-year-old turn-of-the-century German villa with a four-story modern structure, bringing together old and new, history and modernity.

"We see ourselves as a place where the past, present and future are all explored in equal measure," Sabena Donath, the institution's director, told DW.

Donath and her co-director, Doron Kiesel, view the academy as "a bridge between academia and the general public" and as "a home for scholars and a home for those who ask questions."

Donath said the aim was to put the focus on topics related to the philosophy of religion and ethics as well as on topical debates concerning contemporary Jewish life.

The program aims to reflect the many facets of Jewish life and the diverse forms of Judaism. 

Kiesel told DW: "We want to show how Jews live today and how heterogeneous Jewish life is. And that it is completely wrong to speak of 'the' Jews or 'the' Jewish way of thinking."

Ahead of the opening, the president of the Central Council of Jews also named interfaith dialogue as one of the institution's topics, and, in an interview with the German newspaper, the Frankfurter Allgemeine, Schuster expressed the hope that the academy would bring into the public sphere "Jewish themes besides the topic of antisemitism and Jewish persecution.”

But these issues will also be on the agenda. "We have,” said Kiesel, "a problem in this country that antisemitism is concealed behind numerous topics, but keeps on resurfacing, sometimes more evidently, sometimes more subtly.”

The project grew out of an initiative from the former head of the Central Council Dieter Graumann, who encouraged the setting up of an educational department in 2012. Its work was shaped by the directors of the new institution.

Security measures push up price tab

A mezuzah — a small capsule containing verses from the Torah intended to serve as a reminder of God's commandments — is affixed to the entrance of the academy. Security measures are also an integral part of this new building.

"It is a bitter reality that Jewish institutions must be guarded," said Donath. The academy is being protected just as Jewish schools and synagogues must be protected. "For us, this is a sad reality of everyday life."

The construction costs of around €40 million ($45 million) — about half of which was covered by the Central Council of Jews and half by the federal and state governments — ended up being significantly higher than calculated at the groundbreaking in 2021, partly due to the structural security measures.

entries.title: Cristiano Ronaldo announces retirement from international football
entries.summary: The announcement by the footballing legend comes just weeks after a public spat with Portugal coach Jorge Jesus over playing time.
entries.content:
November 5, 2026

The announcement by the footballing legend comes just weeks after a public spat with Portugal coach Jorge Jesus over playing time.

Cristiano Ronaldo took to social media on Thursday to announce that he had played his last game for Portugal.

"To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the number seven shirt of our national team," the 41-year-old Ronaldo said in a video on his Instagram account.

"I never felt it belonged to me alone, but for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world."

The former Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus forward represented his country 234 times, scoring 146 goals — making him the men's record-holder for ⁠international ​appearances and for international goals.

Decision made with 'head and heart'

He captained Portugal ​to their first major trophy at ​Euro 2016 and led them to the 2019 and 2025 Nations League titles.

"It was not an easy decision, there are decisions that are not ​only with the head. They are also made with the heart," Ronaldo continued in the Instagram post.

"If I ever made you happy, ​if one of my goals ever made you hug someone, forget a worry or feel ⁠proud ​of our country, then it ​was all worth it."

He also thanked his family, the Portuguese people ​and the teammates, coaches and staff he worked with over his national ​team career.

'The greatest of all time'

The Portuguese Football Association (FPF) released a statement expressing its gratitude and respect for the player also known as "CR7."

"Cristiano Ronaldo has raised Portugal's profile and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps; for many of us, he is the greatest player of all time!" it read.

The FPF intends to organize a tribute "in which the fans and the country can one more time applaud and celebrate a player who has given us so much."

Training camp walkout

While his long-rival Lionel Messi ended his Argentina career with a much anticipated farewell match last month, Ronaldo's final appearance may go down as Portugal's 1-0 win over Wales on September 24, depending on the nature of the tribute. Portugal coach Jorge Jesus left him on the bench for the following match and said he wouldn't start the next one.

Ronaldo responded by walking out of the Portugal training camp. He was subsequently suspended and fined by the FPF, but he had been expected to return to Portugal for the November international break.

Like Messi, Ronaldo intends to continue his club career with Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia.

entries.title: North Korea tells EU to 'mind its own business' on human rights
entries.summary: North Korea's UN mission has lashed out at the European Union over a draft UN resolution. Pyongyang has said the West does not have a monopoly on human rights.
entries.content:
North Korea

North Korea tells EU to 'mind its own business' on human rights

November 5, 2026

North Korea's UN mission has lashed out at the European Union over a draft UN resolution. Pyongyang has said the West does not have a monopoly on human rights.

North Korea, responded European Union's draft United Nations resolution on human rights in the country by telling the bloc to "mind its own business," state media reported Thursday.

Pyongyang has long been accused by the UN and human rights advocates of committing human rights violations.

North Korea's UN mission said in a statement carried by the official Korean Central News Agency that the move was a "farce" and a "politically motivated provocation."

It said the resolution is "flagrantly distorting it's human rights policy," claiming that human rights are not "a monopoly of the West."

Referring to the protests in Europe, "Streets are filled with demonstrators from all walks of life demanding such elementary rights as the rights to existence," the North Korean mission said.

"The EU had better mind its own business, instead of hyping up the non-existent 'human rights issues,'" it added.

South Korea to co-sponsor the resolution

The UN General Assembly has adopted a resolution condemning North Korea's human rights violations every year since 2005.

According to the South Korean Yonhap News Agency, Seoul has decided to co-sponsor the resolution proposed by the EU.

It is the fifth consecutive year that Seoul has done so, following a break from 2019 to 2021 under the liberal Moon Jae-in government. 

The draft text is expected to be adopted by the Third Committee of the UN General Assembly later this month, before being submitted to the UN General Assembly for final approval.

entries.title: Poland arrests four over alleged spying for Russia
entries.summary: Poland has charged four people with espionage, saying they were sending information to Moscow. Two more have been accused of shipping military components to Russia.
entries.content:
November 5, 2026

Poland has charged four people with espionage, saying they were sending information to Moscow. Two more have been accused of shipping military components to Russia.

Polish authorities said Thursday they had arrested six people over alleged military component shipments to Russia, four of whom they charged with espionage.

Investigators said the group illegally supplied Moscow with significant quantities of parts used to manufacture ammunition and weapons systems despite an embargo.

What are the suspects accused of?

Four suspects, including the Russian woman, were charged with espionage and placed in pretrial detention for three months, Poland's Internal Security Agency (ABW) said. The other two are subject to non-custodial restrictions.

All six also face allegations of violating rules governing international trade in goods and technologies of strategic importance to national defense and international security.

"Russia is subject to a strict embargo in this area, and this operation was designed to circumvent it," Siemoniak told reporters.

The suspects are five Poles aged 25 to 52 and a 37-year-old Russian woman, intelligence coordinator Tomasz Siemoniak said.

Why is Poland concerned about Russian operations?

Poland, an EU and NATO member, is a major supporter of Ukraine and the main transit route for Western military and humanitarian aid to the country.

Siemoniak said nearly 100 people had been charged in ABW espionage and sabotage investigations since January 1, 2024.

Warsaw has repeatedly accused Russia of sabotage since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. On Tuesday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Poland had foiled a possible provocation at its border with Russia's Kaliningrad exclave.

The Russian Embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Kremlin has consistently denied conducting sabotage operations in NATO countries.

entries.title: Finland court jails captain and crew member over Baltic cable sabotage
entries.summary: Finland seized the Fitburg freighter last year over the suspected sabotage of cables linking Helsinki and Tallinn. It's one of several incidents of damaged infrastructure in the Baltic since Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
entries.content:
November 5, 2026

Finland seized the Fitburg freighter last year over the suspected sabotage of cables linking Helsinki and Tallinn. It's one of several incidents of damaged infrastructure in the Baltic since Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

A Finnish court on Thursday convicted the Russian captain and a senior crew member of the cargo ship Fitburg for damaging two undersea telecommunications cables in the Gulf of Finland last year.

The Helsinki District Court found the two defendants guilty of "aggravated criminal damage."

It said in a statement that they had intentionally dragged the ship's anchor along the seabed for around 130 kilometers (81 miles).

The captain was sentenced to three and a half years in jail, while the crew member, an Azerbaijani citizen, was sentenced to two years and 10 months.

They were also ordered to jointly pay around €1.9 million ($2.1 million) in damages, the Reuters news agency reported, with the captain to pay about €85,000 more.

The defendants denied any wrongdoing and have challenged Finland's jurisdiction in the case.

What else do we know about the Fitburg freighter?

Finnish authorities seized the vessel on December 31 on suspicion that it had damaged cables linking Finland's capital, Helsinki, and Tallinn, Estonia.

Finnish police at the time said the ship had been dragging its anchor for hours when it was discovered in Finland's exclusive economic zone.

The Fitburg and its 14-member crew had been en route to the port of Haifa, Israel, from the Russian city of St. Petersburg when the incident occurred.

Finland has stepped up efforts to protect its undersea infrastructure following a series of incidents involving cables and pipelines in the Baltic Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

entries.title: Several European flights receive bomb threats, some divert
entries.summary: At least a dozen flights were either diverted or landed with a military escort after bomb or security threats. The first reported case involved a flight from Dublin to Rome landing outside Paris and more soon followed.
entries.content:
France

Several European flights receive bomb threats, some divert

November 5, 2026

At least a dozen flights were either diverted or landed with a military escort after bomb or security threats. The first reported case involved a flight from Dublin to Rome landing outside Paris and more soon followed.

At least a dozen commercial flights made either unscheduled or high-alert landings in Austria, France, Italy, Belgium, Czechia, Spain and Bulgaria, according to authorities in the various countries.

Planes made unscheduled landings in Evreux, France; in Vienna, Austria; and in Bulgaria. A flight from Finland landed in Rome as scheduled but with a military escort, and various others touched down at their scheduled destinations across the continent but amid security alerts.

The incident in France became public knowledge first, but the other similar reports soon followed.

No initial signs of a genuine threat, EU says still 'too early' to say if cases linked

This comes after a series of bomb threats leveled against several European flights earlier this week, prompting similar unscheduled landings. 

Tuesday's incidents turned out to be hoaxes, and preliminary information shows no sign of dangerous materials reported in Thursday's threats as yet.

The European Union Commissioner for Transport and Tourism, Apostolos Tzitzikostas, wrote online that any threats against civilians were unacceptable.

"It is too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked," Tzitzikostas said. "National investigations remain ongoing."

What happened in the subsequent alerts across Europe?

Finland's Finnair carrier reported that two planes landed at their scheduled destinations but amid security scares.

One Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome landed with a military escort, according to Italian news agency ANSA. Another plane from the Finnish capital, operated by Jettime, also landed in Vienna as scheduled.

A Wizz Air flight from Milan to Warsaw made an unscheduled landing in Vienna.

Bulgaria reported three aircraft making emergency landings because of bomb threats.

Three Ryanair flights to Sofia — from Copenhagen, Madrid and London Stansted — also all landed under high alert. Two of them touched down in Sofia as scheduled and one diverted to Plovdiv, the airport's CEO said.

Italian news outlets and the Reuters news agency reported, citing airport sources, that two planes — an Aegean Airlines flight from Thessaloniki and a Ryanair flight from Porto — landed at the Malpensa airport in Milan as scheduled after receiving bomb alerts on Thursday morning.

Police in Madrid said that three flights at the Spanish capital's airport were affected by what they called hoax threats, saying that security forces searched the area and ruled out any risk.

Police in the Czech Republic later said that they were preparing officials at Prague airport for four landings after threats of improvised explosive devices being on board.

"We assess the relevance of the threats as low," police said. "Nevertheless, we do not underestimate the threat, which is why all necessary security measures have been activated with the least possible impact on passengers and airport operations."

Police said the planes would be swept for dangerous materials on landing.

What do we know about the first incident outside Paris?

An Airbus A320 plane has been diverted to the Evreux airbase to the west of Paris following a bomb threat.

The office of French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu announced the incident on Thursday, saying it was monitoring the situation "in real time."

The flight was headed from Dublin, Ireland, to the Italian capital of Rome.

Tracking websites showed the plane, part of the Aer Lingus fleet, sharply deviating its course as it was around Paris' airspace and heading towards the more isolated airfield in Evreux.

France's air force said that it dispatched planes "as soon as the incident was reported."

"The aircraft has been diverted and is being escorted to Evreux airfield," it said.

Lecornu's office subsequently confirmed that the plane, part of the Aer Lingus fleet, had landed safely at the airfield.

What happened during the earlier disruptions?

The prior threats to commercial flights this week turned out to be hoaxes that nevertheless caused diversions and major security mobilizations.

In one case, the Italian air force escorted a plane to its emergency landing.

The threats targeted airlines including Poland's LOT, Scandinavian Airlines, Wizz Air and Ryanair.

While it's not yet clear if there is a link, these disruptions to commercial aviation also coincided with a series of apparent cyberattacks targeting freezer units in major supermarkets and even French bloodbanks. 

All the cases remain nascent, but have the potential hallmarks of so-called hybrid attacks designed to cause maximum disruption with minimal effort and resources.

entries.title: South Korea tests Arctic shipping route amid Russia-West row
entries.summary: For South Korean ships, navigating off the north coast of Russia dramatically reduces travel time to Europe, but the pro-Ukraine coalition might see it as undermining their efforts to isolate Moscow.
entries.content:
South Korea

South Korea tests Arctic shipping route amid Russia-West row

November 5, 2026

For South Korean ships, navigating off the north coast of Russia dramatically reduces travel time to Europe, but the pro-Ukraine coalition might see it as undermining their efforts to isolate Moscow.

A South Korean container ship completed a voyage to Western Europe through the Arctic Ocean off the northern coast of Russia in October, fueling Seoul's hopes of exploiting the route as a shortcut for trade.

The ship made the round trip from Busan to Rotterdam in just 50 days, saving at least 10 days compared to the fastest travel times along the more commonly used Suez Canal route. The Northern Sea Route (NSR) is not only around 7,000 kilometers (4,350 miles) shorter, it also avoids the geopolitical flashpoint of the Middle East.

But the faster delivery times might not exactly trigger celebrations across western European capitals.

Analysts say the nations arrayed against Russia over its invasion of Ukraine fear that South Korean President Lee Jae-myung is looking to boost Seoul's economic relations with Moscow. This would run contrary to the efforts to cut off Russia made by Kyiv and its Western alies.

One of the reasons for South Korea testing the Arctic route is its undoubtedly large economic potential. But analysts told DW that Seoul also hopes that, by having a working relationship with the Russian regime, they could sway its leader Vladimir Putin against providing more weapons to North Korea.

Lee's government, they suggest, will need to navigate the geopolitical waters extremely carefully.

Climate change opening up NSR

The container vessel PanStar Acro left the South Korean port of Busan on August 22 and navigated around Russia to reach the southern British port of Felixstowe, then continued its journey by sailing to Rotterdam in the Netherlands and Gdansk in Poland, before heading back along the NSR.

For decades, the NSR was impassable due to the North Pole ice cover. With the ice in retreat due to climate change, navigation is becoming possible, although commercial ships often need to be accompanied by an ice-breaker vessel at certain times of year.

According to the Arctic Council, an international body which includes the US, Russia, Canada, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Denmark and Iceland, last year saw a record 1,812 vessels operating in the Arctic. That marks an increase of 40% compared to 2013.

The NSR "presents significant economic potential" for South Korea by linking it more closely to the key markets of Europe while bypassing the challenging waters of the northwest Indian Ocean, said Joseph Kristanto, a maritime security analyst at Singapore's S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies.

"In addition to potentially lowering shipping costs and transit times, the route's development could strengthen Busan's position as a regional maritime hub and create opportunities for South Korea's shipbuilding sector."

The Lee government has outlined plans for regular commercial services on the NSR by 2030, with the first Korean ship to complete the voyage merely a test of the logistics.

Fears of 'strategic dependency'

The danger, however, is that by developing the NSR as South Korea's favored route to Europe, "it could introduce a new form of strategic dependency on Russia as Moscow exercises considerable control over navigation along its Arctic coastline," said Kristanto.

"From the European perspective, closer economic engagement with Russia risks undermining efforts to isolate Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine."

Kristanto pointed out that Moscow could apply pressure through regulations and "the provision of icebreaker assistance.”

The analyst also said that European diplomats' concerns over Seoul's recent engagement with Moscow go beyond the NSR and include the alleged delivery of around 165,000 tons of fuel — aboard sanctioned Russian tankers — to Russia in August.

All of this is happening as Pyongyang, Seoul's archrival, is sending troops to help Russia in its war against Ukraine.

Was Seoul's row with Kyiv a calculated move?

"South Korea is very interested in accessing the NSR as climate change means that a route that was previously impossible to use is now accessible and makes perfect economic sense," said Andrei Lankov, a Russian-born professor of history and international relations at Seoul's Kookmin University.

At the same time, Seoul is "trying to send signals to the Russian government that it is willing to manage relations," he added.

It also coincides with Seoul taking a firmer stance against Ukraine, a position that dates back to September, when President Volodymyr Zelenskyy addressed the UN General Assembly and confirmed that two North Koreans who had been taken prisoner in Ukraine had been moved to South Korea. Seoul reacted angrily and claimed that Zelenskyy had violated an agreement to keep the transfer of the two POWs secret.

The dispute degenerated into a major diplomatic spat, with Seoul demanding apologies and ultimately withdrawing a number of its diplomats from Kyiv.

Lankov believes the row may have been somewhat performative on Seoul's part as it allowed Lee's administration to distance itself from Kyiv and resist pressure to provide material help to Ukraine. He said this stance would have been appreciated in Moscow.

"And then Russia could reciprocate by not providing North Korea with advanced and dangerous military technology," Lankov added.

Korea keeps low profile while waiting for Ukraine war to end

"Right now, South Korea wants to fly under the radar, to examine the possibilities and be prepared for when the war is over, and sanctions on Russia are lifted in the future," said Lankov. "That's the economic plan, but they are also hoping that by working with Moscow they can halt the transfer of more weapons to the North."

Kristanto also expects Seoul to "pursue a cautious and incremental approach."

"Seoul is unlikely to abandon the initiative altogether, particularly given growing Chinese interest in Arctic shipping, but it will also seek to avoid unnecessarily antagonizing its Western partners," he said.

"Ultimately, South Korea is not necessarily choosing between Russia and the West, but attempting to preserve a potentially valuable economic opportunity without compromising its more fundamental strategic relationships."

entries.title: Germany news: Deportations on the decline
entries.summary: Despite a decrease in overall deportations, more people were sent back to Turkey. Volkswagen is facing a fresh 'Dieselgate' trial. And Germany's leading DAX stock index hit a new high. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Deportations on the decline

Published November 5, 2026last updated November 5, 2026

Despite a decrease in overall deportations, more people were sent back to Turkey. Volkswagen is facing a fresh 'Dieselgate' trial. And Germany's leading DAX stock index hit a new high. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Official numbers show a strong decline in deportations in 2026 compared to last year
  • Germany's leading DAX stock index reached a record high following the US midterms
  • More than ten years after the 'Dieselgate' scandal, a new trial is set to begin against former Volkswagen executives

Here are the latest headlines from across Germany on Thursday, November 5: 

Skip next section One in three German companies still intends to cut spending: survey

One in three German companies still intends to cut spending: survey

Despite increasing signs that Europe's biggest economy is recovering after several tough years, a new study shows that one in three companies in Germany still plans to slash investments in 2027.

"Only one in five manufacturing businesses plans to expand capacity - only half as many as in 2018," said the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry (DIHK), which surveyed companies across the country.

Additionally, the DIHK found that for most firms planning to spend in the next fiscal year their money will largely be spent on replacing machinery and equipment rather than innovation or development.

"As long as private companies do not invest more again, neither more growth nor new jobs will be created," said DIHK chief Helena Melnikov.

Recently, data showed that after two years of recession, the German economy is expected to grow by 1.3% by the end of 2026 and that trend should continue into next year.

Melnikov cautioned, however, that "this growth has been bought with taxpayers' money and new public debt. State aid must not obscure the deep structural problems of Germany as a business location."

"Anyone who wants sustainable growth again must release the brakes on investment and innovation," she added.

Skip next section Government reaches deal for public ownership of tank manufacturer — report

Government reaches deal for public ownership of tank manufacturer — report

Business daily Handelsblatt has reported that the federal government has reached a deal with the  KNDS defense firm for a takeover of the German part of the business by the state.

Although headquartered in the Netherlands, KNDS is a holding company for French weapons maker Nexter and the German defense company Krauss-Maffei Wegmann (KMW).

Up until now, KMW, a major tank manufacturer, has been family-owned and controlled.

Handelsblatt said it had received a copy of an agreement, labeled "confidential," which states that the German government will now have a 50% stake in the business.

The deal has long been in the works, but this was the first confirmation that negotiations were finished.

Skip next section Autopsy ordered for Bavarian deputy premier

Autopsy ordered for Bavarian deputy premier

Authorities in Berlin have ordered a full autopsy for Hubert Aiwanger, the economy minister and deputy premier of Bavaria, who was found dead in his hotel room in the German capital late on Wednesday.

Officials told German news agency DPA that they hope this would determine the 55-year-old's cause of death, which is still unclear.

He had been in Berlin to open a new office for his conservative populist "Free Voters" party, which rules in a coalition with the Christian Social Union (CSU) in Bavaria. The CSU is the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

Known for his antagonistic political style, Aiwanger has made a name for himself despite his party's small standing on the federal level — including accusations of being far-right and antisemitic.

Those who had seen him prior to his death said he had been complaining of not feeling well and had canceled an appearance due to health concerns.

Skip next section DAX marks record high after US midterms

DAX marks record high after US midterms

Germany's leading DAX stock index hit a record high on Thursday morning, reaching 26,644.33 points. The previous record, set in August, was about 30 points lower.

Most European stock markets recorded an increase on Thursday due to optimism following the results of the US midterm elections. This is partly due to President Donald Trump's signaled willingness to work with a Democrat-controlled Congress and the perception that regulatory and trade policy will now be less erratic.

This was also coupled with a slight ease in oil prices, after the Trump-led war with Iran sent fuel costs skyrocketing in recent months.

Skip next section Government seeks to plug gaps in swimming and driving lessons

Government seeks to plug gaps in swimming and driving lessons

The federal government is set to give the German Swimming Association some €20 million ($22.5 million) over a four-year period in order to get more young children into swimming lessons.

A recent survey found that more than half of elementary school children cannot swim properly, prompting concerns about their safety around water.

In recent decades, lack of funding in infrastructure has seen public swimming pool closures around the country, with people in rural areas especially having to travel further to reach increasingly crowded pools. This was compounded by the COVID-19 pandemic, which saw a number of programs close and never reopen.

In some areas, parents put their children on waiting lists for years for subsidized public swimming lessons or else have to pay exorbitant amounts for private ones.

The Bundestag is also currently debating driving school reforms, which are largely private and usually charge thousands of euros for instruction — increasingly becoming unaffordable for large sections of the German population, yet still required to apply for a driver's license.

Lawmakers hope to finalize the reform soon, which includes more transparent pricing, online theory lessons, and the ability to have some of the required practice hours on the road led by a relative rather than a driving instructor.

Skip next section Harry Kane extends contract with Bayern Munich

Harry Kane extends contract with Bayern Munich

Ballon d'Or winner and England captain Harry Kane has extended his club contract with Bayern Munich, the footballer's team announced Thursday.

"I feel at home at Bayern Munich. I love the club, the fans, the city of Munich. We have a fantastic team and Vincent Kompany is a fantastic coach. It am extremely proud to a part of this club," Kane said of signing on for two more years.

Kane scored an incredible 26 goals in the Bundesliga last year, more than any other player in the league.

Skip next section Police clear students occupying university lecture hall

Police clear students occupying university lecture hall

Police in the central German city of Kassel said on Thursday that they had cleared a student protest overnight, removing some 47 people from a lecture hall.

Three of the "occupiers," were charged over the incident, police said, and the other 44 were released after officers documented their identities.

However, "all 47 are being investigated for disturbing the peace," the authorities added.

The students were protesting changes the University of Kassel has made to what is called the "civil clause" employed by most public German universities. It is part of the university charter that ensures all research at the institution is conducted solely for civil purposes and never for military or corporate interests.

University officials have said that the change to their civil clause is part of their new "peace initiative," and simply seeks to clarify "the difficulty of distinguishing between civilian and military purposes within this research institution."

Skip next section 'Dieselgate' back in the courtroom

'Dieselgate' back in the courtroom

More than 10 years and many lawsuits and investigations later, the Volkswagen 'Dieselgate' scandal has once again landed in front of a judge. 

Also referred to as the Volkswagen emissions scandal, the news broke in September 2015 that the German auto giant had been using a "defeat device" to cheat United States emissions tests.

Thursday's proceedings in Braunschweig are the latest in a series of legal battles against several former VW executives who have appealed their sentences.

There is also the case of then-CEO Martin Winterkorn. He resigned in the wake of the scandal but has not faced any legal consequences. After years of investigations, his trial was delayed multiple times by the COVID-19 pandemic, and then by health issues. It remains unclear when his trial will restart.

Skip next section Overall deportations down, but returns to Turkey on the rise

Overall deportations down, but returns to Turkey on the rise

The number of people deported from Germany decreased by nearly 19% from January to September 2026 compared to the previous year, the Interior Ministry announced following a request from the Left Party.

Some 14,324 people were deported in the first nine months of this year, down from 17,651 in 2025. Turkey was the most common destination, followed by Georgia and Algeria.

The numbers reveal that deportations to Syria remain difficult due to the political situation there, even for convicted criminals. Six people have been returned there since the beginning of 2026.

Deportations to Turkey, however, appeared to buck the trend, as 2,025 people have been sent there.

According to the Interior Ministry, the number of foreign nationals leaving the country voluntarily has also slightly increased. Some 14,140 people have received assistance to return to their countries of origin, compared to 12,263 the year before.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Good morning from a crisp and autumnal Bonn.

Today we will be bringing you stories about a decline in deportations, corporate scandal and whether Germans will be able to learn to swim and drive — and how much it might cost.

Stay tuned!

entries.title: France braces for fresh protests as unions strike over higher wages
entries.summary: Unions representing the education sector, rail employees, public hospitals and postal services called the strike. Authorities have deployed some 70,000 police and security officers across the country.
entries.content:
France

France braces for fresh protests as unions strike over higher wages

November 5, 2026

Unions representing the education sector, rail employees, public hospitals and postal services called the strike. Authorities have deployed some 70,000 police and security officers across the country.

Hundreds of thousands of people marched in French cities on Thursday, as public workers staged a strike alongside protesting students.

The mobilization, called by trade unions seeking higher wages, came after demonstrations over education and the rising cost of living on October 17 triggered some of the worst rioting France has seen in years.

Police were out in force for Thursday's protests, with Interior Minister Laurent Nunez announcing around 70,000 police officers and security forces would be deployed across the country.

Unions said that around 260 rallies were planned nationwide. Authorities estimated some 500,000 to 700,000 people would take part in the demonstrations, including about 80,000 in the capital, Paris.

Protests in Marseille, Lyon, Paris

Demonstrations kicked off in the southern cities of Marseille and Lyon, and Nantes in the west, on Thursday morning.

An official close to Interior Minister Nunuz was cited by the Associated Press as saying that most of the rallies were peaceful, but that there was some violence in Lyon, Nantes, Pau, Orleans, Rennes and Toulouse.

Authorities in the western region of Brittany said "masked individuals" had tried to block roads in the city of Rennes.

BFM TV reported that a high school near the southwestern city of Toulouse was set on fire.

The main protest in Paris began at 2 p.m. local time (1300 GMT).

Reuters reported that high school students and other protesters had already faced off against riot police in the French capital on Thursday morning after they blocked a street with rubbish bins.

Who is striking on Thursday?

Public and private education unions called for staff to walk off the job, as well as unions representing rail workers, public hospitals and postal services.

They are demanding an increase in the minimum wage, across-the-board wage raises, tax reforms and better learning conditions for young people.

The Education Ministry said just over 15% of French teaching staff went on strike. French power unions also joined the action, state-owned utility EDF said.

The Eiffel Tower was ​shut on Thursday because of the strike.

Media reports said state railway operator SNCF expected only minor disruptions to long-distance services. It was not immediately clear to what extent a strike called by air traffic controllers would disrupt air traffic.

Among those joining Thursday's marches were students who have been protesting for weeks over deteriorating learning conditions. Those demonstrations have grown to include widespread anger over high living costs and inequality.

Although the recent student-led protests have largely been peaceful, some saw clashes with police, with officers using tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds, as well as rioting and looting.
